items.title: Hackers Exploiting Plex Vulnerabilities in the Wild to Deploy Cryptominer Malware
items.summary: Hackers are exploiting flaws in Plex Media Server to install cryptocurrency mining malware, with a researcher recording successful attacks against a honeypot on October 17, 2026. The activity follows the release of Plex2Shell, a public exploit that chains four vulnerabilities to run code without logging in. Later observations also revealed proxy software running alongside the miner. The findings from Boredhackerblog show active exploitation of an exposed test server, rather than scanning alone. However, the available evidence does not establish how many real servers have been compromised or identify the attackers behind the activity. The researcher also warned that restrictions on outbound traffic initially prevented collection of some payloads. How the Plex2Shell Exploit Works Plex announced security updates on September 1, urging users to install Plex Media Server 1.43.3 and Plex Desktop 1.115.0. Its official security notice warned that NAS users might need to install updates manually. Cyber Security News previously covered the Plex security update and affected releases . The exploit combines CVE-2026-96652, CVE-2026-96654, CVE-2026-96655, and CVE-2026-96656. According to the Plex2Shell repository , the chain starts with server-side request forgery, which tricks Plex into sending requests chosen by an attacker. It then reaches internal functions, gains access to owner-authorized requests, and writes a file to an attacker-selected location. The final stage abuses the loading of an unsigned codec to execute code. The repository identifies versions before 1.43.3.10828 as vulnerable and lists 1.43.3.10861 as fixed. Although the exploit supports Linux and Windows targets, the reported honeypot activity involved a Linux-based Plex deployment running in Docker. Honeypot Captures Miner and Proxy Activity In the researcher’s report , the first exploitation attempt came from 45.194.92[.]222. Further attempts involved 91.92.40[.]202 and 176.65.139[.]228. Recorded requests targeted /player/timeline/subscribe and included references to internal Plex services, an sslip.io hostname, and the Python-urllib/3.10 user agent. After outbound access was enabled, the researcher observed downloads from 217.60.194[.]116 involving files named docker and x . Published artifacts included packed and unpacked samples, followed by an XMRig miner. Similar misuse of XMRig has appeared in other campaigns, including attacks against exposed Redis servers . An update also reported a process named myawesomeproxy and traffic involving proxystream[.]st. The program displayed a message about external use of the device’s internet traffic. These observations raise concerns about proxy abuse, but they do not establish who operates this Plex campaign or prove a connection to a specific botnet. items.summary_html:
Hackers are exploiting flaws in Plex Media Server to install cryptocurrency mining malware, with a researcher recording successful attacks against a honeypot on October 17, 2026.

The activity follows the release of Plex2Shell, a public exploit that chains four vulnerabilities to run code without logging in. Later observations also revealed proxy software running alongside the miner.

The findings from Boredhackerblog show active exploitation of an exposed test server, rather than scanning alone. However, the available evidence does not establish how many real servers have been compromised or identify the attackers behind the activity. The researcher also warned that restrictions on outbound traffic initially prevented collection of some payloads.

How the Plex2Shell Exploit Works

Plex announced security updates on September 1, urging users to install Plex Media Server 1.43.3 and Plex Desktop 1.115.0. Its official security notice warned that NAS users might need to install updates manually. Cyber Security News previously covered the Plex security update and affected releases.

The exploit combines CVE-2026-96652, CVE-2026-96654, CVE-2026-96655, and CVE-2026-96656. According to the Plex2Shell repository, the chain starts with server-side request forgery, which tricks Plex into sending requests chosen by an attacker. It then reaches internal functions, gains access to owner-authorized requests, and writes a file to an attacker-selected location.

The final stage abuses the loading of an unsigned codec to execute code. The repository identifies versions before 1.43.3.10828 as vulnerable and lists 1.43.3.10861 as fixed. Although the exploit supports Linux and Windows targets, the reported honeypot activity involved a Linux-based Plex deployment running in Docker.

Honeypot Captures Miner and Proxy Activity

In the researcher’s report, the first exploitation attempt came from 45.194.92[.]222. Further attempts involved 91.92.40[.]202 and 176.65.139[.]228. Recorded requests targeted /player/timeline/subscribe and included references to internal Plex services, an sslip.io hostname, and the Python-urllib/3.10 user agent.

After outbound access was enabled, the researcher observed downloads from 217.60.194[.]116 involving files named docker and x. Published artifacts included packed and unpacked samples, followed by an XMRig miner. Similar misuse of XMRig has appeared in other campaigns, including attacks against exposed Redis servers.

An update also reported a process named myawesomeproxy and traffic involving proxystream[.]st. The program displayed a message about external use of the device’s internet traffic. These observations raise concerns about proxy abuse, but they do not establish who operates this Plex campaign or prove a connection to a specific botnet.

Administrators should install the latest Plex release and verify the running version, particularly on NAS systems and Docker deployments. On Linux, review the Plex process tree for unexpected child processes, suspicious downloads, and unfamiliar mining or proxy programs. The researcher recommends examining processes with ps axjf.

Defenders can use the published packet captures to develop detections. Files marked “lab” come from controlled tests, not live attacks. The repository also warns that attackers can change ports, domains, and filenames, so matching only fixed indicators will leave detection gaps.

An EDR alert reveals an attack. But can it tell the full story? Discover how to reconstruct the attack timeline.

items.title: Microsoft Confirms October Windows Updates Can Break Exchange Server Email Services
items.summary: Microsoft has confirmed that Windows Server security updates released on October 13, 2026, can disrupt Exchange Server email services, blocking webmail access and leaving messages undelivered. The issue affects some on-premises systems running Exchange Server 2016, Exchange Server 2019, and Exchange Server Subscription Edition. Microsoft has published a workaround and advises administrators not to uninstall the Windows updates. The failures stem from changes in Windows Server, not the separate October Exchange Server security updates. Servers can experience problems even without installing the latest Exchange patches, making the underlying operating system update the key factor when investigating these outages. Affected Updates and Exchange Server Symptoms Microsoft identified four Windows updates linked to the failures. These are KB5126646 for Windows Server 2025, KB5126655 for Windows Server 2022, KB5126651 for Windows Server 2019, and KB5126868 for Windows Server 2016. The impact depends on server workload, and some systems may never develop symptoms. Users may be unable to sign in to Outlook on the web, while messages sent through Outlook remain stuck in the Outbox. Administrators may notice growing mail queues, failed mailbox access during replication, or problems with Database Availability Group members reaching quorum. Restarting an affected server may restore service temporarily. One error administrators should watch for is MapiExceptionMdbOffline: Unable to make connection to the server. (hr=0x80004005, ec=1142) . Affected systems may also record Event ID 1006 in the Application log, providing a useful sign when checking whether an outage matches Microsoft’s report. According to Microsoft’s Windows release health notice , the October updates introduced a default limit of 512 simultaneous Endpoint Lookup calls. This limit controls memory use by Endpoint Mapper, a Windows component involved in remote procedure call communications. Heavy Exchange workloads can exceed the default allowance. Increasing the limit allows Endpoint Mapper to use more memory to handle these calls. Microsoft currently lists the issue as mitigated rather than resolved and says its investigation remains ongoing. An additional mitigation is available through Microsoft Support for affected organizations. Microsoft’s Registry Workaround Microsoft’s Exchange Team advisory instructs administrators to open an elevated Command Prompt on the Exchange server and run reg add "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Rpc" /v EpmapSavedContextCap /t REG_DWORD /d 65536 /f . The server must then be restarted. After the reboot, administrators should monitor the environment for recurring failures. Microsoft says the limit should be raised further if problems return, although its advisory does not specify a second value. The company reports that this approach has resolved the issue in customer cases it has handled. Keeping security updates installed remains important. The disruption also arrives as Exchange 2016 and 2019 approach the end of their final paid update period. Following earlier reporting on out-of-support Exchange servers , Microsoft says October 2026 marks their last scheduled ESU security release, with future updates limited to Subscription Edition. Affected Updates and Exchange Server Symptoms

Microsoft identified four Windows updates linked to the failures. These are KB5126646 for Windows Server 2025, KB5126655 for Windows Server 2022, KB5126651 for Windows Server 2019, and KB5126868 for Windows Server 2016. The impact depends on server workload, and some systems may never develop symptoms.

Users may be unable to sign in to Outlook on the web, while messages sent through Outlook remain stuck in the Outbox. Administrators may notice growing mail queues, failed mailbox access during replication, or problems with Database Availability Group members reaching quorum. Restarting an affected server may restore service temporarily.

One error administrators should watch for is MapiExceptionMdbOffline: Unable to make connection to the server. (hr=0x80004005, ec=1142). Affected systems may also record Event ID 1006 in the Application log, providing a useful sign when checking whether an outage matches Microsoft’s report.

According to Microsoft’s Windows release health notice, the October updates introduced a default limit of 512 simultaneous Endpoint Lookup calls. This limit controls memory use by Endpoint Mapper, a Windows component involved in remote procedure call communications. Heavy Exchange workloads can exceed the default allowance.

Increasing the limit allows Endpoint Mapper to use more memory to handle these calls. Microsoft currently lists the issue as mitigated rather than resolved and says its investigation remains ongoing. An additional mitigation is available through Microsoft Support for affected organizations.

Microsoft’s Registry Workaround

Microsoft’s Exchange Team advisory instructs administrators to open an elevated Command Prompt on the Exchange server and run reg add "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Rpc" /v EpmapSavedContextCap /t REG_DWORD /d 65536 /f. The server must then be restarted.

After the reboot, administrators should monitor the environment for recurring failures. Microsoft says the limit should be raised further if problems return, although its advisory does not specify a second value. The company reports that this approach has resolved the issue in customer cases it has handled.

Keeping security updates installed remains important. Cybersecurity News recently covered Microsoft’s reissued Exchange Server security update, highlighting the continuing need for supported patches.

The disruption also arrives as Exchange 2016 and 2019 approach the end of their final paid update period. Following earlier reporting on out-of-support Exchange servers, Microsoft says October 2026 marks their last scheduled ESU security release, with future updates limited to Subscription Edition.
